raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of heart failure that affects women of childbearing age [1]. It is defined by the development of left ventricular systolic dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] < 45%) presenting in the late stages of pregnancy or in the early postpartum months, in the absence of any other identifiable cause of heart failure [2]. The global incidence of PPCM varies widely, with a disproportionately high burden in regions such as South Africa and Haiti, and among women of African descent in the United States [3, 4]. Other key risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, particularly preeclampsia [5, 6].

The pathophysiology of PPCM is complex, currently conceptualized as a multi-factorial "two-hit" process involving systemic angiogenic imbalance, oxidative stress, and hormonal triggers [7]. A pivotal mechanism involves the cleavage of the hormone prolactin. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, the protease cathepsin D cleaves full-length 23-kDa prolactin into an angiostatic and pro-apoptotic 16-kDa fragment [8]. This 16-kDa prolactin fragment impairs endothelial cell function, induces capillary dissociation, and disrupts myocardial metabolism [9]. Additionally, late-pregnancy secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) by the placenta further compromises the maternal vasculature, compounding myocardial injury [10]. Genetic susceptibility also plays a significant role. Truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*), similar to those observed in dilated cardiomyopathy, are present in up to 15% of PPCM cases [11, 12]. Furthermore, cellular and molecular investigations have identified microRNAs, such as microRNA-146a, as both crucial mediators of this pathological cascade and potential diagnostic biomarkers [13]. Other molecular pathways, including the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and its downstream effectors, are essential for protecting the maternal heart from peripartum stress [14].

PPCM typically presents with symptoms of congestive heart failure, such as dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and peripheral edema, which can easily be mistaken for normal physiological changes of late pregnancy or the postpartum state [15, 16]. Consequently, delays in diagnosis are common, contributing to increased morbidity [17]. Diagnostic evaluation requires a thorough clinical assessment, electrocardiography, and measurement of natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) [18]. Transthoracic echocardiography remains the gold standard, demonstrating an LVEF of less than 45%, frequently accompanied by left ventricular dilation [19].

Therapy for PPCM must balance maternal benefit with fetal safety when initiated antepartum. Standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure should be optimized [20]. During pregnancy, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated due to fetotoxicity; instead, a combination of beta-blockers (such as metoprolol succinate), hydralazine, and nitrates is utilized [21]. Postpartum, management can be transitioned to standard GDMT, including sacubitril/valsartan and MRAs [22].

In addition to conventional heart failure regimens, targeting the prolactin cleavage pathway with bromocriptine—a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion—has emerged as a disease-specific disease-modifying therapy [23]. Clinical trials have shown that adding bromocriptine to standard GDMT improves LV recovery and clinical outcomes [24, 25]. Anticoagulation is recommended when bromocriptine is used, and in patients with severely reduced LVEF, due to the high risk of thromboembolism associated with the hypercoagulable postpartum state. For patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF < 35%) at risk of sudden cardiac death, the temporary use of a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) provides a safe "bridge to recovery" during the initial months of medical optimization, avoiding premature permanent implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement [26, 27].

While PPCM carries significant risks, its prognosis is generally more favorable than other forms of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, with up to 50–70% of patients exhibiting substantial or complete recovery of LV function within six months [28]. However, patients with persistent LV dysfunction face a high risk of adverse events in subsequent pregnancies, including severe heart failure recurrence and death [29]. Subsequent pregnancy in women who have fully recovered their LVEF (>50%) also carries a risk of relapse, necessitating extensive preconception counseling and close multidisciplinary monitoring [29, 30].
